title: Ro-Ro and Car Carrier Inspection: Bow Doors, Ramps and Car Decks
description: How ro-ro ships, ro-pax ferries and car carriers are inspected: bow, side and stern doors under UR S8, S9 and Z24, ramps, car decks and hull surveys.
h1: Inspecting Ro-Ro Ships, Ro-Pax Ferries and Car Carriers: Shell Doors, Ramps and Vehicle Decks
intro: Ro-ro ships load through openings in the hull. Bow, side and stern doors, ramps and the long undivided vehicle decks behind them are what make the trade work, and they are also where a ro-ro ship is most exposed. Class treats the doors as safety-critical, with design rules in UR S8 and UR S9 and survey requirements in UR Z24. This guide covers ro-ro cargo ships, ro-pax ferries and pure car and truck carriers: what the door rules ask, where doors, ramps and car decks wear and crack, and what owners and buyers check.

highlights.h: Doors keep the sea off the vehicle deck
highlights.p: A vehicle deck has no internal subdivision to limit water that gets in. Securing, supporting and locking devices, seals, indicator lights, television surveillance and leakage detection together keep shell doors closed and prove that they are, which is why each one is examined.

highlights.h: Ramps and car decks are moving structure
highlights.p: Stern and internal ramps, liftable car decks and their hoisting gear combine structure, hinges, wires and hydraulics that work at every port call. Fatigue at hinges and supports, wear in pins and contact damage from vehicles are the findings that recur from ship to ship.

highlights.h: The register matters as much as the steel
highlights.p: Each ship keeps an operating and maintenance manual with a register of inspections, repairs and renewals of door securing, supporting and locking devices. Surveyors and buyers read that register alongside the structure, because it shows how wear has been managed over the years.

sections.h: Why do shell doors decide the safety of a ro-ro ship?
p: Most cargo ships keep the sea out with a continuous deck and hatch covers well above the waterline. A ro-ro ship has large openings in its shell close to the waterline at the bow, stern or side, and behind them a vehicle deck running most of the ship's length without transverse bulkheads. Water that enters can run from side to side across that deck, and its free surface quickly erodes stability. The door requirements are built around three ideas: the doors must be strong enough for the sea loads, they must be held shut by devices that cannot work loose, and the bridge must know at all times whether they are closed and locked.

The same logic explains the inner door. Under UR S8 the inner door, which may be a vehicle ramp placed for the purpose, forms part of the collision bulkhead, so a damaged or open outer door still leaves a second barrier between the sea and the vehicle deck.

sections.h: Bow doors, inner doors, side doors and stern doors: what is examined?
p: Bow doors are either visor type, lifted upwards about hinges on the foredeck, or side-opening, swinging outwards in two leaves. Side shell doors abaft the collision bulkhead serve side ports on ro-pax ships and car carriers, and stern doors close the after end, often combined with the stern ramp. UR S8 and UR S9 use the same three terms for all of them: a securing device keeps the door closed by preventing it from rotating about its hinges, a supporting device transmits loads from the door to a securing device and on to the ship's structure, or straight to the structure as a hinge or stopper does, and a locking device locks a securing device in the closed position. Inspectors examine each group separately, because each fails in its own way.

sections.h: Which rules govern ro-ro doors? UR S8, UR S9 and UR Z24
p: UR S8, Bow Doors and Inner Doors, and UR S9, Side Shell Doors and Stern Doors, set design requirements for ro-ro passenger ships and ro-ro cargo ships on international and domestic voyages, other than high-speed light craft. They cover strength, the arrangement of securing, supporting and locking devices, indication and monitoring, and the operating and maintenance manual. Their survey counterpart is UR Z24, Survey Requirements for Shell and Inner Doors of Ro-Ro Ships, applied at the periodical class surveys. The rest of the hull is surveyed under UR Z7, Hull Classification Surveys, since ro-ro cargo ships are among the types excluded from the general dry cargo requirements of UR Z7.1.

Under UR Z24 the annual survey covers the door structure and the shell around each opening, hinges and bearings, close-up survey of the securing, supporting and locking devices and their welds, clearances that can be measured without dismantling, seals and drainage, a complete opening and closing test, and tests of the indicators, leakage detection and television surveillance, with a hose test or equivalent that ro-ro cargo ships may omit when the examination and function test are satisfactory. The special survey adds wider clearance measurement, dismantling of the drainage non-return valves, and non-destructive testing and thickness measurement of the securing, supporting and locking devices as the surveyor considers necessary; diminution of those devices and the hinging arms is limited to 15 per cent of the as-built thickness or the society's corrosion allowance, whichever is less. The surveyor reads the operating and maintenance manual and its register before starting.

sections.h: Indicator lights, television surveillance and leakage detection
p: UR S8 requires separate indicator lights and audible alarms on the navigation bridge and at the operating panel to show that bow doors, inner doors and their securing and locking devices are properly closed. The system is fail-safe, with a lamp test, and a harbour and sea voyage mode sounds an alarm on the bridge if the ship leaves harbour with a door not closed or a securing device out of position. Television covers the space between the bow door and the inner door, with monitors on the bridge and in the engine control room, leakage through the inner door raises an alarm, and water collecting in that space is drained with a bridge alarm at a set level.

UR S9 applies similar indication to side and stern doors bounding special category or ro-ro spaces where flooding could occur. Passenger ships need leakage detection with an audible alarm and television reporting to the bridge and engine control room, cargo ships an audible alarm on the bridge. For inspection, the sensors are the weak point: proximity switches knocked out of alignment, cabling damaged at hinges, fogged camera housings and blocked drains behind the bow door. Functional tests with the crew show whether each signal is genuine.

sections.h: Hinges, locks and cylinders: where do doors wear and crack?
p: Door hardware wears every time it moves and every time the sea loads it. Hinge pins and bushes wear oval, the door drops or shifts, seals stop compressing evenly and securing devices start carrying loads they were not designed for. Locking pins and housings wear, cleats lose their bite, and hydraulic cylinders weep at their seals and work loose at their lugs. Slamming on a bow visor in head seas concentrates load at the hinges, lifting arms and lower locks, and cracks start at the weld toes of lugs and brackets.

The inspection records clearances at hinges and locks against the maker's limits, examines lug and bracket welds by eye and confirms indications with magnetic particle testing, checks pins and bushes when they are drawn, and reads the repair register for patterns: the same lock repaired at every docking points to misalignment, not a bad part. Seal tightness on doors closing against packing can be checked ultrasonically, following the maker's seal arrangement.

sections.h: Stern, quarter and internal ramps: what fails?
p: Ramps carry every vehicle that boards. A stern or quarter ramp is a hinged steel structure, often in two or three folding sections with flaps or fingers at its outer end, raised by wires and sheaves or by hydraulic cylinders. The hinge connection to the ship is the critical detail: fatigue cracks start in the hinge lugs, the transom structure behind them and the ramp's own hinge girder, and pin wear lets the ramp work under traffic. Flaps and fingers are bent by quay contact, ramp plating dents under heavy axles, and wires, sheaves and their foundations wear and crack.

Internal ramps between decks on car carriers and ro-pax ships bring the same issues on a smaller scale, with cracking where fixed ramps meet the decks they join and wear at the hinges of ramps that also close openings between decks. Wires, winches and hydraulics are maintained under the maker's instructions by the crew; the structure, hinges and foundations are where crack detection and thickness readings help.

sections.h: Liftable car decks, pillars and vehicle deck structure
p: A pure car and truck carrier has many vehicle decks, several of them liftable panels raised or lowered to suit high and heavy cargo. The panels rest on brackets or pins on the side shell, casings and pillars, and the usual findings are worn or cracked support brackets, bent locking pins, panels distorted by overloading or impact, worn hoisting wires and seized deck locks. Fixed car decks use thin plating on light stiffeners, so corrosion and dents erode their margin quickly, especially where seawater and road salt drip from vehicles and condensation forms in cold weather.

The main vehicle deck, usually the freeboard deck, carries trailers and heavy units and is examined for deformation, wastage and cracking at deck girders and pillars. D-rings and flush lashing sockets are welded attachments checked for cracks and for wastage of the deck around them. Scuppers, drains and their non-return valves matter because water left on a vehicle deck is a stability issue as well as a corrosion one. Fire doors, drencher pipework, ventilation openings and insulation are noted visually where damage is seen, without testing; those systems are surveyed under SOLAS chapter II-2 and by class.

sections.h: Hull surveys and thickness measurement on ro-ro ships
p: Hull surveys on ro-ro ships follow UR Z7, so the thickness measurement minimum grows from suspect areas at special survey No. 1, to a transverse section of deck plating at No. 2, two sections with the peak tank internals at No. 3 and at least three sections from No. 4. On a ro-ro ship those sections cut through vehicle decks, side casings and double-bottom tanks, and the gauging plan adds areas peculiar to the type: heeling tanks used to keep the ship upright during loading, the shell and frames around side door openings, the transom in way of stern door and ramp hinges, and vehicle deck plating where water lies. Under UR Z3 the outside of the bottom is examined at least twice in each five-year period, at intervals not exceeding 36 months.

Ballast tanks, heeling tanks included, go on annual examination under UR Z7 when a hard coating is POOR and not renewed, when soft or semi-hard coating is used, or when no hard coating was applied at construction. On ro-pax ferries with many port calls and short passages, an owner's inspection timed to a lay-by period or short docking lets structure be gauged and crack-checked without disturbing the timetable.

sections.h: What owners and buyers check on a ro-ro ship or car carrier
p: An owner preparing for a class survey, or a buyer before a sale, starts with the operating and maintenance manual and its register of inspections, repairs and renewals of securing, supporting and locking devices. UR S8 and S9 recommend recorded inspections of the supporting and securing devices by ship's staff monthly and after heavy weather or contact damage, so gaps in the register are informative. Then come the class records for the doors, earlier crack detection and clearance reports, ramp and car deck repair history, hoisting system condition and thickness trends for vehicle decks and ballast tanks. On board, functional tests of doors, indicators, alarms and cameras with the crew are followed by close inspection of hinges, locks, ramps and decks.

faqs.q: What is the difference between UR S8 and UR S9?
faqs.a: UR S8 covers bow doors and the inner doors behind them, which form part of the collision bulkhead. UR S9 covers side shell doors abaft the collision bulkhead and stern doors opening into enclosed spaces. Both apply to ro-ro passenger ships and ro-ro cargo ships, define securing, supporting and locking devices in the same way, and require indication on the bridge and an operating and maintenance manual.

faqs.q: How often are ro-ro shell doors surveyed?
faqs.a: Class examines shell and inner doors at every annual survey under UR Z24, with a function test, indicator and alarm tests and close-up survey of the securing, supporting and locking devices; the special survey adds wider clearance measurement and non-destructive testing and thickness measurement of those devices as the surveyor considers necessary. Between surveys the door rules recommend recorded inspections of supporting and securing devices by ship's staff monthly and after heavy weather or contact, with damage reported to class.

faqs.q: What are securing, supporting and locking devices on a ro-ro door?
faqs.a: A securing device keeps a door closed by stopping it rotating about its hinges. A supporting device transmits external or internal loads from the door to a securing device and on to the ship's structure, or directly to the structure, as a hinge or stopper does. A locking device locks a securing device in the closed position. The rules treat them separately because each carries load differently, and an inspection checks the wear, fit and condition of each group in turn.

faqs.q: Why does the bridge need door indicators and cameras?
faqs.a: Because a door that looks closed from a distance may not be secured, and on a ro-ro ship sailing with a door open means water on an undivided vehicle deck. The indicator panel shows whether doors and their securing and locking devices are in position, an alarm sounds if the ship leaves harbour otherwise, and television and leakage alarms show what is happening behind the bow door.

faqs.q: Can ultrasonic testing check the seals of ro-ro doors?
faqs.a: Yes, on doors that close against compressed packing. A transmitter on one side and a receiver run around the frame on the other show where the seal is not seating. The method suits weathertight shell doors and many internal closures, is planned around the door maker's seal arrangement, and its results sit beside the clearance and wear measurements that explain why a seal leaks.

faqs.q: What fails on car carrier decks?
faqs.a: Liftable decks suffer worn or cracked support brackets, bent locking pins, distorted panels and worn hoisting wires, often from high and heavy cargo placed beyond the deck's design load. Fixed decks are built from thin plating, so dents and corrosion from seawater and road salt reduce their margins quickly. Lashing points, scuppers and drains are checked on every deck.

faqs.q: Who can take thickness readings on a ro-ro ship for class?
faqs.a: Readings that count towards a class survey need a thickness measurement firm holding UR Z17 approval from the ship's classification society, working under the attending surveyor's control. Owner's readings and crack detection taken before a survey or a sale need no such approval, and they give the owner the information needed to plan the docking scope and any steel or door repairs.
